title: Zechariah 13:1–6
context: The oracle that began in chapter 12 continues, and the LORD of Armies speaks of that day. A fountain will be opened to David’s house and the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and uncleanness, following the promise that the LORD will pour out a spirit of grace and supplication and that they will look to him whom they have pierced (12:10). John 19:37 cites 12:10 at the crucifixion: “They will look on him whom they pierced.” Revelation 1:7 echoes it; these uses are named without being merged with Zechariah. The LORD will cut off the names of idols and remove the prophets and the spirit of impurity from the land (compare Hosea 2:17). Anyone who still prophesies falsely will be condemned by his own parents, as the law required for one who speaks lies in the LORD’s name (Deuteronomy 13:6–9; 18:20). False prophets will be ashamed, will stop wearing the hairy mantle (compare 2 Kings 1:8), and will deny being prophets (compare Amos 7:14). Verse 6 asks about wounds between the arms; many interpreters take these as self-inflicted marks of a false prophet (compare 1 Kings 18:28), while some older Christian readers applied the line to Christ, and the context makes the first reading the more common one today. Shared ground: Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as a promise of cleansing and of the end of idolatry and false prophecy.

verses.text: “In that day there will be a fountain opened to David’s house and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a fountain opened for sin and uncleanness to David’s house and Jerusalem. Cleansing is offered freely to the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fountain following the outpouring of grace in 12:10. Shared ground: both traditions generally read it as a promise of God’s cleansing, which many connect with Christ (compare 1 John 1:7).

verses.text: It will come to pass in that day, says the LORD of Armies, that I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they will be remembered no more. I will also cause the prophets and the spirit of impurity to pass out of the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD of Armies cutting off the names of idols and removing false prophets and the spirit of impurity. Worship will be purified.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God himself removing idolatry from the land (compare Hosea 2:17). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as hope for purified worship.

verses.text: It will happen that when anyone still prophesies, then his father and his mother who bore him will tell him, ‘You must die, because you speak lies in the LORD’s name;’ and his father and his mother who bore him will stab him when he prophesies.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see parents condemning a child who prophesies lies in the LORD’s name. Loyalty to God outweighs even family ties.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of the law’s judgment on false prophets (Deuteronomy 13:6–9; 18:20). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse in its covenant setting, not as a pattern for private action today.

verses.text: It will happen in that day that the prophets will each be ashamed of his vision when he prophesies; they won’t wear a hairy mantle to deceive,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see false prophets ashamed of their visions and no longer wearing the hairy mantle to deceive. Deception will lose its power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the outward marks of prophecy no longer used to mislead (compare 2 Kings 1:8). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as the exposure of false religion.

verses.text: but he will say, ‘I am no prophet, I am a tiller of the ground; for I have been made a bondservant from my youth.’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a former false prophet denying his role and claiming to be a farmer. Shame drives him to disown his claims.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of Amos 7:14, now used to disown false prophecy. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as showing false prophecy brought to an end.

verses.text: One will say to him, ‘What are these wounds between your arms?’ Then he will answer, ‘Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers commonly take the wounds between the arms as marks of a false prophet, explained away as injuries among friends. Some read the line differently.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many now read the wounds as a false prophet’s marks (compare 1 Kings 18:28), while some older readers applied the line to Christ. Shared ground: both traditions generally hold the reading with care.
